questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8]}^{′}}{[{x}^{2}]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}^{′}}{[2x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[-\frac{1}{(x+4)\sqrt{x+4}}]}{2} \\  & =\frac{[-\frac{1}{(0+4)\sqrt{0+4}}]}{2} \\  & =\frac{[-\frac{1}{4(2)}]}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=1$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)}{{x}^{2}-2x+1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{[2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)]^{′}}{[{x}^{2}-2x+1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)}{2x-2} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)}{{x}^{2}-2x+1} & =-{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)}{x-1} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{[\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)]^{′}}{[x-1]^{′}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)}{1} \\  & =-{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & ={\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡4x=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4x}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\operatorname{ln}⁡4x]^{′}}{{[x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{x} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)]}^{′}}{[\operatorname{cot}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}{-{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}{(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡0\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})=-\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{-\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)]^{′}}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{(\frac{3}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{x}^{-1}}{3{x}^{-1}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
